in writing ‒ the main objective of this initiative is to provide tax authorities with consistent and continuous access to information on money laundering. the reduction of tax evasion and avoidance, including in relation to money laundering, must be an absolute priority for the european union and its member states. law enforcement agencies operating in this area need to be facilitated and actively assisted in identifying the true recipients of illicitly obtained funds. the quality of the material equipment and the associated use of the most modern information and communication technologies must be taken for granted. only these will make it possible to trace money laundering activities at an early stage.
in writing ‒ tax evaders always target less transparent regimes and exploit their weaknesses. in order to limit such possibilities and to ensure a level playing field between member states, a common set of rules is needed to enable tax authorities to fulfil their monitoring obligations. tax fraud and evasion harm the economy of the union and its member states and are closely linked to corruption, non-transparency, money laundering and the promotion of terrorism and organised crime. i therefore supported the ep's motion for a resolution amending the council directive regulating the access of tax authorities to information to combat money laundering. sufficient staffing and equipment of tax and customs authorities, mandatory automatic exchange of information, international cooperation of authorities in the field of taxation, consistent legislation for the banking and financial sector, including tracing the beneficial owners of companies, are means to achieve international tax transparency. member states shall bring their legislation into conformity with this directive by 31 december 2017 at the latest.
in writing ‒ all the recent revelations from luxleaks to the panama papers to the bahamas leaks clearly demonstrate that we are dealing with a global phenomenon that requires greater tax transparency and much closer cooperation between jurisdictions. i therefore unambiguously support the proposal for the amendment of the money laundering directive presented by the commission in july this year. we have succeeded in incorporating into the directive the strong requirement that the fight against tax evasion and avoidance should be a top priority for the union. as it appears that there may be a direct link between tax evasion, tax avoidance and money laundering, it is essential that competent authorities are able to cooperate effectively. in the directive we therefore ask member states to make the most of the synergies resulting from national, union and international cooperation between the authorities involved in the fight against crime and abuse. the automatic, mandatory and continuous exchange of information in the field of taxation, which is introduced by this directive, is an important aspect and should apply from january 2018. this will ensure maximum transparency and provide the authorities with a basic tool to prevent and combat fraud of all kinds. as the problem of tax avoidance is global, international coordination is indispensable for an effective fight against money laundering.
in writing ‒ large-scale tax fraud is carried out through sophisticated schemes across borders and across multiple entities. it is important that the control authorities have access to all relevant data for their detection. european cooperation in this area will help to detect them more quickly and save taxpayers money.
in writing ‒ i supported the legislative resolution on the proposal for a council directive amending the directive on access to information by tax authorities for the purpose of combating money laundering. this fight must be the eu's absolute priority. the revelations in the panama papers, the bahamas leaks and so on are proof that there is a need for greater transparency in the tax area and, of course, for closer cooperation between the criminal justice authorities of the various states. practices such as money laundering cross national borders, so i believe that the exchange and sharing of information is absolutely key. we need the various tax authorities to communicate and cooperate with each other, which will lead to increased transparency. especially today, when the public is very sensitive to and reacts to any non-transparent and dubious financial activities, especially in relation to public procurement, effective legislation is essential. indeed, it is often the uncooperative authorities and shell companies in tax havens that are the common denominator of tax fraud.
in writing. ‒ the proposal for a european parliament resolution reflects the annual activity of the european central bank in 2015. the report gives a balanced assessment of the ecb's annual activity, its monetary policy, the risks of low interest rate policies and the need for structural reforms. the primary objective of the european central bank is to maintain price stability by creating a stable investment environment. in 2015, the euro area was faced with a serious challenge of high unemployment, excessively low inflation, macroeconomic imbalances and low productivity growth, which resulted in structural reforms being delayed, investment declining and domestic demand weakening. increasing the competitiveness of the european economy and a credible fiscal policy can be achieved primarily through socially balanced and primarily effective structural reforms that directly promote investment and job creation.
in writing ‒ in principle, i see no problem in extending the expansionary monetary policy as practised and proposed by the ecb, but the ecb alone cannot stimulate aggregate demand unless it is complemented by the necessary investments and ambitious and socially balanced structural reforms at member state level. the ecb can also do more in the area of aid to smes. in view of the current world situation, it is very sad that the impact of the ecb's measures on the real economy has been very limited, banks have been able to access financing at virtually zero or very low costs.

in writing ‒ although 2015 was a year of recovery for the euro area economy, the euro area continues to suffer from high unemployment, excessively low inflation and significant economic imbalances, including current account imbalances. nevertheless, i supported the resolution because i think that the european central bank (ecb) managed to restore consumer confidence in 2015 to support consumption, business confidence to restore job creation and investment, and bank confidence to increase lending. i also take a positive view of the fact that the confidence boost in 2015 was crucial to supporting the recovery and returning inflation to our target of below but close to 2%. i am pleased that the euro area has started to pick up the pace of credit growth and that we continue to see employment growth. on the other hand, however, i must point out that the euro area has not yet been able to cope with the very low level of labour productivity growth that is the result of a lack of investment. i am aware that the euro area is currently facing some uncertainty, particularly as regards the outlook for the world economy and the future direction of europe. however, i believe that the ecb will be able to guarantee price stability in the period ahead and thus achieve the union's objectives.

in writing. ‒ in recent years, the security situation both within europe and in the surrounding region has deteriorated significantly and posed unprecedented challenges. at present, terrorism, hybrid threats, organised crime, cyberattacks and climate change are the main security threats. these challenges cannot be addressed by any single member state or organisation alone. in this situation, the eu must do everything in its power to ensure the safety of its citizens. the increasingly negative perception of risks and threats in europe makes the establishment of a european defence union urgent. the report stresses that europe needs political will and determination to guarantee its long-term security. it also urged the eu member states to make use of the possibilities offered by the lisbon treaty for the common security and defence policy, in particular through permanent structured cooperation. a meeting of defence ministers should be established within the council to provide permanent political leadership and coordinate the development of a european defence union. the defence union must be effectively funded and coordinated with nato. i am convinced that the union must take decisive action to protect the union and its citizens, and i therefore voted in favour of adopting the report.
in writing ‒ there is no doubt that the european union's primary task is to ensure the security of its citizens, which should be backed up by a strong military capability. however, i do not agree with the european defence union proposal because most eu member states are members of nato, where the states do not pay compulsory contributions to each other anyway, and i see no reason for a parallel structure that will cost taxpayers in europe billions of euros.
in writing ‒ the terrorist attacks in europe demonstrate the need for closer union cooperation in the field of defence and security. in addition to coordinated and more effective cooperation, the common defence policy also eliminates the duplication of eu and member state costs for certain activities. i supported the proposal to establish a european defence union, which should be built on the basis of the law in force, mutual cooperation, respect for the rights of the member states and cooperation with the international defence communities. i consider strengthening the union's security and defence capability a priority, which will also increase the citizens' diminished confidence in the union's ability to act.

in writing. ‒ water transport plays a key role in connecting the different regions of the european union in an environmentally friendly and more energy-efficient way of transport, which can also include the use of new, innovative technologies such as solar and wind energy, and therefore greater emphasis should be placed on waterborne passenger transport in the union. in line with the cop21 agreements, it is important that better use of available capacities in the area of waterborne passenger transport not only helps to reduce congestion and co2 emissions, but also improves air quality and provides better transport services overall. it can also help boost tourism along rivers and waterways and thus attract economic growth even in a less well-known region. i voted in favour of the report.
in writing ‒ there is no doubt that the european union is under-using the potential of passenger water transport. road infrastructure in europe has long been overburdened, and we must therefore look for ways to lighten it while helping the environment by reducing greenhouse gas emissions. europe's geographical features include its many rivers, waterways, estuaries, long coasts and islands, which offer exceptional opportunities for water transport. there are many areas in europe where travelling by ferry or cruise ship would be more sustainable, easier and faster, while enhancing the social and economic well-being of the region, protecting europe's environment and the health of its citizens. this is why we should invest much more in research and innovative technologies in shipping in the future, and use the cohesion fund, the structural funds and the regional funds.

in writing europe's geographical conditions offer great possibilities for water transport. passenger ships play an important role in the mobility of eu citizens, with more than 400 million people passing through eu ports every year. efficient use of available water transport capacity would have several positive effects. not only would congestion be reduced, but co2 emissions would be reduced, air quality would be improved and, therefore, better transport services in general would be provided. it is a great positive that eu legislation on the safety of passenger ships has been introduced in recent years, particularly in response to accidents, which has allowed for better protection of the lives of passengers in eu waters and facilitated possible rescue actions. safety has also been enhanced by the introduction of common eu safety standards - now met by most national passenger vessels. however, there is still room for improvement in simplifying the regulatory framework, removing obsolete requirements. although shipping is one of the most sustainable modes of travel, there is further potential, for example, to produce more environmentally efficient vessels through investment in research and innovation. i support the motion with my vote.

member of the commission. – madam president, the figures on adult skills levels in the union are striking. for both economic and social reasons, we urgently need to act. weak reading and writing is a problem for one fifth of european adults, while another quarter has difficulty with numeracy, and – even in this digital age – up to 40% of adults have low or no digital skills. they are effectively cut off from the digital age, unable to find information online or to buy a train ticket on the web, for example. because of their low skills levels, their chance to have a job is lowered, their income is lower and their livelihood and health are at risk. this is why we must show our determination to help the most vulnerable in society. they need a strong foundation of basic skills and the opportunity for a true second chance. this is why we propose the skills guarantee, a skills guarantee for adults to develop their basic skills and progress towards higher qualifications. at the heart of this initiative is the idea that adults need flexible pathways which allow them to combine learning with their other – sometimes complex – responsibilities. i welcome the fact that, yesterday, ministers reached a political agreement on the commission proposal – and this in less than 6 months. i regret, however, that our proposed title has been diluted by the council, which decided to call this now upskilling pathways: new opportunities for adults. the core elements of our proposal have been preserved. as you know, these are built on three practical steps and a strong partnership approach. turning to the questions you raise on the action plan for the implementation, our original proposal required each member state to draw up a detailed action plan for implementing the recommendation. during the negotiations in the council, this was replaced with a more general text, but also invited member states to outline appropriate measures for implementation at national level by mid-2018 at the latest. i hope that member states will attach the appropriate importance to its implementation. we stand ready to support them and will take stock of national implementing measures by the end of 2018. the advisory committee on vocational training will work with the commission to follow up this initiative, and this tripartite body brings together government and social partners and representatives from all member states. regarding funding, as you know, the provision of basic skills is – and remains – a national competence and should be funded first and foremost by national sources. this should be prioritised in national budgets. the recommendation does not require member states to start from scratch; our proposal builds on their existing policy and practices. the commission has made clear from the start that there is no additional eu funding. nevertheless, considerable eu funds are already available for use by member states on education and training, employment and social inclusion. we have eur 27 billion of esf funding that will be invested in education, training skills and lifelong learning from 2014 to 2020. in addition, eur 21 billion is available for social inclusion, and eur 30 billion for sustainable and high-quality employment, which can also support the integration of people with low skills. i also want to use the opportunity to thank parliament for having defended so effectively the budget increase of the erasmus+ programme for 2017, as well as the youth employment initiative. it demonstrates that political priorities are not only based on words: to make a real change, policies need to be transformed into concrete actions and be supported by adequate funding. in fact, most member states have already prioritised low—skilled adults in their esf operational programmes, including supporting adult learning in libraries, in community centres, and, among others, on the factory floor. regarding the commission’s strategy to involve member states, at european level there is already a forum that can follow up the initiative, as mentioned already: the tripartite advisory committee on vocational training. the adult learning strengths of the erasmus+ programme will support suitable projects on peer learning between member states. we will work closely with member states in supporting as needed esf interventions targeting low—skilled people. we will also continue through the european semester to emphasise the importance of upskilling and reskilling adults. as you remember, in 2016 not less than 10 member states received country—specific recommendations in this area. education, training and skills will continue to be covered in the detailed report on each country and therefore provide a regular opportunity for the commission to highlight the issues raised by this initiative, whether or not they lead to a country—specific recommendation. regarding literacy as a reason for school dropout, this initiative complements the extensive work carried out by the commission together with member states and stakeholders to prevent early leaving from education and training. as you know, we aim to reach the european benchmark of 10% or less of early leavers from education and training by 2020. we are already supporting mutual learning among member states and improving the evidence base, thanks to the expertise of cedefop and eurydice. this new recommendation focuses on addressing the consequences of early leaving by providing a second chance to adults who were failed in previous decades and left school without acquiring a sound level of basic skills or qualifications. this must be part, too, of our shared commitment to fight inequalities in society, to combat poverty and to help break the cycle of inter-generational poverty, including by giving parents opportunities to improve their skills. the adoption by the council of this recommendation and the agreement reached yesterday is just the first step. now the main challenge is translating this political commitment and ambition into concrete measures for citizens which make a difference in their lives. we are ready to work together to make this happen.
for the ecr group although slovakia is among the european union countries with a relatively low number of pupils who leave school early, the trend is rising, unlike in other eu countries, and this is not good news. because people without a high school education are among the most vulnerable groups. in slovakia, only 34% of them are able to find employment, and therefore we need to adjust the conditions of the education system so that these people also have the opportunity to acquire qualifications and skills in secondary education. the guarantee of skills should follow the guarantee for young people, whose potential we have unfortunately not been able to fully exploit in slovakia. i therefore hope that, also on the basis of good experiences from other member states and the commission's recommendations, the skills guarantee will bring more tangible results. because behind every single number in the statistics on the number of students who drop out of school early is the fate of a particular person, and everyone has a right to a second chance.
in writing, i supported the 2018 parliamentary calendar because, despite the reservations of many eu citizens, we meps must also respect the existing treaties and meet 12 times in strasbourg. moving 751 meps, assistants, officials, etc. from brussels to strasbourg every month costs a considerable sum of money from the eu budget. but for that to change, all eu member states must agree, including france, where the plenary meetings are held. to save money, we tried to reduce the number of meetings in strasbourg by setting one meeting for monday and tuesday, no meetings on wednesday and a second meeting on thursday and friday. we wanted to comply with the treaty article which stipulates that we meet in strasbourg 12 times a year, but in fact we would only travel six times. this was eventually challenged by the european court of justice, and even though there were two meetings, only one session was counted. the alternation of weeks, when committees, political groups and plenary meet, is a good system because there is enough time to prepare, debate and debate motions for resolutions before we vote in plenary.
‒ the european parliament's calendar of business is established annually on a proposal from the conference of presidents. it comprises 12 four-day sessions in strasbourg, 6 two-day sessions in brussels, two weeks a month for meetings of parliamentary committees and interparliamentary delegations, one week a month for meetings of political groups and four weeks a year for the work and activities of meps in their constituencies.
in writing ‒ i did not support the motion for a resolution requesting an earlier opinion of the court of justice on the eu-canada agreement. further postponement of ratification of the agreement is damaging to the union's economy and business environment. i am of the opinion that doubts can be treated contractually by a legal provision.
in writing. ‒ i rejected the motion for a resolution, firstly because i am completely satisfied with the content of the agreement to be concluded with canada, and secondly because we risk our credibility by tricks to delay the adoption of the agreement. last spring, the international trade committee asked the same question to the european parliament's independent legal services unit, which gave a clear answer. we have worked on this convention for many years and it is time to put it into effect and start feeling the positive effects.
in writing ‒ parliament rejected the resolution requesting the opinion of the court of justice. since parliament considers that there is no legal uncertainty, it has decided not to request an opinion.
in writing ‒ i did not support the resolution by which some political groups proposed that ceta be referred to the european court of justice. the groups sought to have the procedure relating to the agreement suspended in the european parliament and to wait for the court of justice to give a ruling. the court of justice was required to assess the compatibility of certain elements of the agreement (in particular the investor protection scheme) with european union law. i have decided to vote against this resolution because the european parliament's legal service has already assessed the compatibility of ceta with european union law and has concluded in favour of the agreement. therefore, i see no reason to reassess the compatibility of something that has already been assessed once and with a positive result.
‒ the european union is seen as a leader in the fight against air pollution and climate change. over the last decade, the european union has made a considerable effort to introduce strong legislation. however, several member states still have problems with compliance with the rules and agreed standards. member states must have full information on how they are meeting their emission reduction commitments. where member states are in danger of defaulting, measures should be put in place to identify the problem in a timely manner, allowing countries to take corrective action. it is very important that the european commission plays a comprehensive monitoring and warning role in this regard, by assisting member states with the key elements of their national programme or, in the most serious cases, by enabling them to take the necessary measures. the european commission will have to focus more on regulating the many sectors of the economy that contribute to air pollution in the future. a good example is the automotive industry, where the european commission should present a euro 6c emissions regulation as soon as possible.
in writing ‒ poor environmental and air quality impacts on quality of life, damages the natural environment and vegetation, which impairs the health of the population and increases public health expenditure. the cost of treating air pollution-related diseases in europe is estimated at between eur 330 and 940 billion per year. yet, not all countries are meeting their emission reduction commitments. i support the new directive which sets new national emission ceilings for the five most common pollutants. however, the sanctions must also be reviewed, otherwise the commitments are unenforceable. at the same time, research, science and the development of new measures that will lead to emission reductions need to be supported and financed.
in writing the reduction of emissions to air is an integral part of the european union's environmental policy, in which the union not only fulfils its international commitments but also strives to maintain its position as a world leader in this field. the present report reflects the initiative of the commission and the council to revise the legislation to combat air emissions at national level. the dangerous substances which member states must unconditionally limit to the lowest possible level are in particular sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, volatile organic compounds other than methane and ammonia, solid particles with a diameter of at least 2,5 micrometres and methane emissions. the elimination of these air pollutants is important in relation to the achievement of the 2030 agenda targets. for this reason, all member states are obliged to reduce their national ceilings and to revise their targets regularly (every two years). i believe that all member states and sectors must contribute to the achievement of the commonly agreed objectives, including maritime countries, air transport and shipping. the report has my support.
in writing. ‒ an adult inhales tens of thousands of litres of air a day, yet we tend to forget how important air quality is. air pollutants cause smog and acid rain, have a negative impact on the environment, and contribute to various diseases. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament and the council should be consulted on the draft directive. i am particularly pleased that the report includes areas that have the greatest impact on air quality, such as the automotive industry or agriculture.
in writing ‒ while the eu and its member states have made some progress in reducing air pollution, i too must say that many member states are not meeting all the agreed standards. i therefore voted in favour of the motion for a resolution because i believe that if we are to meet the long-term air quality objectives, we must adopt measures to ensure that pollution from medium combustion plants such as power stations for large buildings and small industrial plants is reduced. like the rapporteur, i support the commission's new commitment to smarter and more efficient regulation and to reducing the administrative burden on businesses and member states. i believe that the ceilings for the target dates set out in the report will not only provide a sufficient incentive to reduce emissions, but will also be set at a level that is realistic, proportionate, feasible and will not have a disproportionate impact on any sector. i also consider it important that the commission should play a comprehensive monitoring and warning role in relation to the fulfilment of emission reduction commitments, thus helping member states to achieve the targets set.
in writing ‒ the fight against air pollution must be undertaken at the level of the european union as a whole. however, it is also necessary to take into account the specificities of each country and to assess the structure of its economy. the emission ceilings for individual pollutants must be set in such a way as not to impair the development of industrial production.
in writing ‒ i supported the report on emissions of certain air pollutants. the report dealt with the revision of the national emission ceilings directive, which is part of the so-called clean air policy package. the new regulation thus sets binding national limits for selected air pollutants for the period up to 2030. air pollution remains a major problem despite the progress made in this area. air pollution is responsible for a host of diseases, premature deaths, and problems caused by subsequent climate change. i therefore appreciate that the revision has set itself ambitious objectives in this regard, which include not only reducing adverse impacts on public health and the environment, but also creating new jobs and developing innovative 'green' technologies.
‒ the resolution in question will influence the forthcoming european union legislation on the banking sector. it is essential that banks play a positive role for society and that they become an effective element of the economy again, rather than a risk element. banks must be of good quality and well capitalised and their main contribution must be to support the real economy, to reduce systemic risk and to try to avoid a repetition of the great economic and financial crisis.
‒ the basel accords have gradually adjusted the capital adequacy rules of banks since 1988. the basel iii rules are a response to the financial crisis of 2008 2009. they detail global regulatory standards for bank capital adequacy and liquidity, enhance risk coverage and introduce measures to promote capital building that can be raised in times of crisis. however, they are not legally binding and need to be transposed into eu law to be effective. the commission notes that the bank of greece has not provided any information on the capital injections of the bank of greece in the period from 1 january 2011 to 31 december 2012. the banking sector has a significant impact on the financing of the union economy, and i therefore support the proposal that the commission should work towards transposing the rules without increasing the administrative burden. strict banking supervision must prevent the savings of the population from being jeopardised and the irresponsible conduct of banks from being covered by common resources. consequently, personal responsibility must also be assumed in this area.
in writing ‒ i supported the resolution calling for the completion of the basel iii framework because i believe it is important that banks are a functional part of the economy. they cannot be a risk to economies, and to avoid the gigantic bank failures we saw during the crisis, banks need to be sufficiently capitalised to support the real economy. the basel committee's work is an attempt to create the conditions for the mitigation of differences between legal environments and banking models. the committee's recommendations, while not binding, are the standard for the banking sector for the central banks of the countries that are members. i also agree with the rapporteur that the eu banking model cannot be penalized and that it needs to be regulated with the same rules for the same level of risk. the resolution we adopted today is a contribution to the basel committee's discussion on the future legislative arrangements for the banking sector. we want to highlight the need for greater transparency and accountability, which would increase the legitimacy of the basel committee. its conclusions should be more closely linked to the work of the european institutions, so that they can be better integrated into the reforms currently under way in the eu. the banking sector has a bad reputation among the people and it would be good if more responsible rules of conduct could be introduced into its operations.
in writing ‒ the basel iii framework aims to increase the simplicity, comparability and convergence of the risk-weighted capital framework in order to address the excessive variability of risk-weighted assets and to apply the same rules to the same risks. the commission should assess the feasibility of a future regulatory framework consisting of less complex, more appropriate and proportionate prudential rules specifically adapted to different types of banking models.
in writing. ‒ the european security environment has deteriorated significantly in recent times, becoming more flexible, more dangerous and less predictable. these threats are taking on more and more different forms. the security of the eu member states is closely interlinked, yet member states react to common threats and risks in a disjointed and fragmented way. a thorough and substantial review of the common security and defence policy (csdp) is needed to address these problems. the report emphasises that the establishment of permanent structured cooperation would allow for the establishment of self-defence or a permanent self-defence structure. stresses that the csdp should be based on the principle of strong collective defence and effective financing, and that the csdp should be implemented in full coordination and complementarity with international institutions with competence in the field of security and defence, such as nato; it believes that the eu should encourage member states to meet nato's capability targets, which require defence spending to be increased to at least 2% of gdp, as confirmed at the wales and warsaw summits. i am convinced that an effective csdp requires a strong commitment and increased and more effective exchange of intelligence and other information between member states, and better cooperation and coordination between member states, especially in the fight against terrorism. since the report points to these things, i voted in favour of it.
‒ europe is facing new challenges to its stability, and we must learn to respond appropriately to them. the security of the member states of the european union is interconnected. however, they often react in isolation to emerging threats, which complicates a common approach. the european union's importance in terms of its foreign policy relevance is not increasing, despite its economic strength and its declared common security and defence policy. the continuing threat of terrorism, but also possible attacks in cyberspace, for example, are putting the standard european way of life under pressure. we need to show common initiative and better coordination in defence and protection of our citizens. otherwise, we will only face a further rise in populism and radicalization. this also applies to investments in research and development in the case of defence technologies. these are naively declining in several member states, despite the growing tensions. we need to eliminate fragmentation and duplication in the european defence sector.
in writing ‒ the threat of military and terrorist attacks is now taking on new dimensions. the use of biological and chemical weapons can threaten entire generations. this is why eu security requires a strong common security and defence policy, based on the principles of prevention, unity, non-aggression and cooperation between the member states of the union, as well as with other defence systems. however, the development of such a policy must not be subordinated to the interests of narrow groups, but must be transparent and credible to the citizens of the union.
in writing the security environment in europe has deteriorated substantially in recent times as a result of conflicts in its neighbourhood. despite the interconnectedness of the security of the union's member states, states react to common threats in an uncoordinated and individual way, making it impossible to take a common approach to crisis management and weakening the union's own position. a more coherent and therefore more effective european foreign and security policy could be beneficial in resolving the conflict in syria and iraq. this will not, however, be achieved without a thorough revision of the common security and defence policy (csdp), which should consist of several steps. it is necessary to establish permanent cooperation structures to enable the union to intervene in different crises and at any stage of the conflict, and this should be based on the principle of robust collective defence and effective financing. the csdp should be implemented in coordination with international security and defence institutions and should be fully complementary to nato. member states should comply with nato's commitments and targets on capability, which require a minimum level of defence spending of 2% of gdp. i support a stronger europe in defence.
in writing. ‒ i support initiatives to strengthen europe's security policy, as we face a growing number of challenges that require decisive and strong action. but we also need to be aware of what is going on around us. after the us presidential elections, we must be aware that the european union's role in nato is far from sufficient. i think we should consider all options before we take the next step.
in writing ‒ i am in favour of strengthening europe's defence capability. but above all, i am in favour of continuing cooperation within nato, where the defence of eu member states, which are also nato member states, is guaranteed by article 5. so in defense policy, i'm all for continuing cooperation within nato. at the same time, i think that eu member states should retain a certain degree of national sovereignty in defence policy. that's why i voted against it.
in writing ‒ i voted in favour of the report on the common security and defence policy (csdp). the situation in which europe finds itself today is extremely unstable. the most acute conflicts are taking place right on our borders. the report attempts to assess the extent to which the csdp has been implemented so far. however, the potential of this framework, which is enshrined in the union treaties, does not seem to be sufficiently exploited. we therefore call on the commission to draw up a white paper on security and defence, and we also welcome the european defence action plan. we stress the need to reform the athena mechanism, which funds eu missions and operations. today, it is the union's missions abroad that are a clear example of how defence cooperation can work at european level. there is no need for a deepened european defence to be the antithesis of nato or to replace it. on the contrary, an independent european defence should cooperate with nato. on the other hand, if we want to think about strengthening and developing european defence industries, we need to ask ourselves where we are going to shift resources from. it is not possible to use funds earmarked for research or regional policy for defence. however, i believe that european defence should be autonomous, so that we can better protect our citizens and the values on which the union is founded.
‒ the security environment in the eu has deteriorated significantly and is becoming increasingly unstable, dangerous and unpredictable. as a result, the common security and defence policy needs to be thoroughly and significantly revised in order to enable the eu and its member states to contribute decisively to the security of the union. one of the instruments is, for example, the creation of a permanent eu headquarters for civil and military missions and operations of the common security and defence policy.
‒ i did not support the report on the implementation of the common security and defence policy. in the light of the current escalating security crises, the report calls for a more effective use of the existing instruments of the common security and defence policy, as well as a strong prevention policy. the report also contains a number of articles calling for stronger cooperation with nato. despite these acceptable requirements, the report discusses the revision of the common security and defence policy, which should aim at permanent structured cooperation to enable the development of common defence. while i am aware that the challenges facing the european union are unprecedented and need to be addressed, i am rather in favour of strengthening cooperation with nato. i think that it is precisely on this cooperation that we should build our defence and not try to create a parallel structure which could ultimately weaken this defence based on cooperation with nato.
in writing ‒ constructive criticism of the european union is very important for its proper functioning. no one's arguing that. it is also why the european union is a successful project that has helped secure more than 70 years of peaceful coexistence in europe. there is still room for improvement, but the prevailing interest of other countries to join is also an important measure. however, objective criticism cannot be confused with the outright lies and propaganda that the eu, its liberal democratic establishment and the member states themselves are exposed to. russia is a key global player. our common interest should be to combat radicalisation and atrocities, which is currently represented by the daesh in particular. but instead of cooperation, we are witnessing a variety of attempts on his part to weaken european cohesion. this is done, for example, through the financial support of populist and far-right parties and movements in individual countries. part of this agenda is also presenting various aspects of the non-democratic establishment and states as stronger than they actually are. incitement to hatred, to restrict the rights of certain groups of the population or to violence cannot be considered as freedom of expression. defending against such behavior, whether on social media or in real life, must be our first priority.
in writing ‒ how the eu deals with information warfare and propaganda depends on the responsibility of each politician, each public official. transparency in action and expression in all policy areas, together with emphasis on the right of citizens to information, quality education, personal accountability and fair punishment for breaking the law, can prevent the spread of lies, unfairness and targeted manipulation.
the european union, its partners, member states and citizens are currently facing an information war from multiple sides. the eu is under pressure from two main propaganda currents: from russia, which is seeking to disrupt the eu integration process, and from its support for anti-eu forces, in particular far-right parties, populist movements that deny the fundamental values of liberal democracy. on the other hand, there is the propaganda of the terrorist organisation da'esh/isis, which promotes political, religious and social hate speech at european and global level. as part of the eu's counter-propaganda measures, the union must strengthen cyber defence and ensure the resilience of eu information systems. member states must cooperate more in the protection of companies. the commission will continue to support the development of the internet and its applications, and will continue to support the development of the internet and its applications. raising awareness of radicalisation is necessary to prevent recruitment, especially of young people. through its external action, the eu should continue to actively promote respect for fundamental rights and freedoms, in particular freedom of expression, assembly, the right of access to the media and the independence of the media in neighbouring countries.
in writing. ‒ it is important that the european union is able to react quickly to any emerging threats. in addition to direct threats to security, we must also deal with attacks on european values. anti-eu propaganda is driven by objectives such as creating doubt, dividing member states and weakening strategic agreements. the most effective tool of the groups behind the propaganda is to instill fear and to restrict the feeling of freedom. the terrorist attacks in europe also convey this message. i support the work of the strategic communications working group and trust that the action plans against propaganda will produce the desired results.
in writing ‒ i abstained from voting on this resolution. my abstention is to say that there are some good things in the document that i stand for, but there are also some things that i can't agree with. i am definitely against propaganda, whether russian or otherwise. however, the document gives equal weight to the so-called islamic state and russia. and i am therefore careful in making such assessments, as i know the situation in the middle east intimately from my personal experience of the region. at the same time, i think it is equally important that the historical facts are not distorted and that the manipulated history is presented to the public and especially to young people, as we are witnessing in my country, slovakia. and i consider this to be gross propaganda.
in writing ‒ although the problem of propaganda from third parties to the union has intensified in recent years, i abstained in the vote on this report. i agree that european countries are under enormous pressure from conspiracy and propaganda websites, but it is not possible to put a state actor, russia, on the same level as a non-state actor, islamic state, in one report. the propaganda to which european citizens are exposed is a fact against which the union will have to define itself by means of a certain strategic communication. but using the same tools to fight radical islamism and to try to define certain parts of europe as traditional russian spheres of influence is not the right approach. the european institutions must act against propaganda with the authorities of the member states, because the situation in each country varies considerably. raising awareness and educating citizens about critical thinking will be key. the digital age is characterised by an information overload that constantly floods citizens. the goal of internet propaganda is to make people feel insecure, confused, and divided. i therefore support the work of the european external action service, which is already doing a good job of detecting and deciphering the disinformation that is being spread daily on the internet.
in writing ‒ russian and islamist propaganda threatens stability and peace in the european union. we cannot fight it with some counter-propaganda, but only with honest politics and open communication with the people. success depends only on the will of the governments of the member states to act in unison. in the case of the slovak one, i have serious doubts whether such a will exists.
in writing ‒ this resolution aims to counter propaganda and attacks on the integrity and values of the eu by both state and non-state actors. they aim to weaken the union from within by instilling fear and creating uncertainty among eu citizens. a special chapter of this resolution is the russian disinformation and propaganda war. in this part, the resolution strongly condemns all the means used by the russian federation to divide europe and create the impression of failing states in its eastern neighbourhood. still, i think it's too early to talk about war with russia. it is true that the eu today faces both direct and indirect russian disinformation pressure. however, the settlement of existing disputes must be based on diplomacy. i therefore do not think it is good that the text of the resolution equates russia with the terrorist group da'esh (isis), although it also skillfully uses propaganda and disinformation to radicalize potential supporters.
in writing. ‒ the resolution adopted by parliament on sign languages and qualified sign language interpreters contributes to ensuring the fundamental right of deaf and hard of hearing citizens to sign language interpretation. sign language interpreting ensures the full participation of the persons concerned in social, cultural and political life, since for sign language users, sign language is their mother tongue. forms of discrimination affecting deaf and hard of hearing people should also be eliminated. i would like to stress in particular the rights of children and those who belong to a minority language community, whose situation requires further positive and supportive impulses at european and member state level. it is very important that services are available to families and children to ensure the rights of minority and sign language children, parents, including access to appropriate education for children.
‒ the european parliament resolution seeks to strengthen and improve the status and situation of sign language, its accessibility, but also to strengthen the role of professional sign language interpreters and thus to be more involved in the fight against discrimination on the grounds of disability.

in writing. ‒ equal treatment for all, including women, children, minorities and people with disabilities, is a fundamental principle of the european union. today we adopted a resolution that makes this possible for people with disabilities. the proposers want to set a good example through the eu institutions in the use of sign language, which they support with recommendations and actions. i welcome the initiative, we've taken another step in the right direction.
in writing. ‒ i support this measure to recognise sign language interpreters, and the important role they play for those without hearing. it has been educational to see sign language used each day with colleagues, enabling full integration into the workplace, and making it possible to draw on the talents of those who would otherwise be excluded. these languages are hard to learn, and must be treasured as part of our european culture, giving a strong message on equality for all.
in writing ‒ i strongly supported the motion for a resolution tabled on the basis of the commission's statement on sign language and professional sign language interpreters. deaf, deafblind and hard of hearing citizens must have the same access to information and communication as others, in the form of sign language interpretation, subtitling, audio-to-text and alternative means of communication, including spoken language interpreters. eu institutions shall set examples of good practice for staff, elected public officials and trainees and towards eu citizens in ensuring appropriate adaptation to needs and ensuring accessibility, including the provision of sign language interpretation. nevertheless, it is urgently necessary to call on all institutions to officially recognise sign language interpreters on an equal footing with spoken language interpreters as regards interpreting services provided to the institutions or their staff and elected public officials, including access to technical support.
in writing ‒ deaf and hard of hearing citizens must have the same access to information and communication as others. parliament therefore stressed the need to increase their support and to strengthen specific provisions such as sign language interpretation and textual information, while ensuring their quality. eu institutions must create examples of good practice.
in writing ‒ the resolution on sign language and professional sign language interpreters addresses the issue of discrimination on the grounds of disability. i support this resolution as people with disabilities have the full right to human dignity and full participation in society. this report addresses the need for sign language to be recognised as an official language in the member states and the eu institutions and the availability of qualified and professional sign language interpreters. it is important that people with hearing impairments have secure access to information and public services. i also welcome the initiative to include sign language in the curriculum to increase awareness of this language. it is precisely society that defines how it treats the most vulnerable.
in writing ‒ i supported the motion on sign language and professional sign language interpreters and was one of the co-rapporteurs. the main objective of this resolution is to achieve the recognition of sign languages as official languages of the member states and of the european institutions. although many people do not realize it, sign languages are a key means of communication for some one million deaf people in the european union. however, interpretation into these languages is rarely provided and interpreters (including in public institutions) are often supplemented by family members of the deaf person. moreover, education in this field is lagging far behind. i therefore think that the recognition of sign languages is an absolutely natural requirement, which also follows from the convention on the rights of persons with disabilities. and the european parliament should set a positive example and make sign language interpreting official.
in writing ‒ this proposal envisages the authorisation of the substance benzazone for a period of 15 years, until 31 january 2032. several studies have shown that the substance benzozone is harmful to the environment. the assessment of the representative uses of the active substance benzazone is not sufficient to conclude that, for at least one of the typical uses, it can be expected that the plant protection product containing the active substance benzazone will not have adverse effects on human or animal health or on groundwater or have an unacceptable effect on the environment. the european commission should focus on verifying the information and making a thorough assessment before taking a decision on approval.
‒ i support the ep's call on the commission to strictly respect the precautionary principle when authorising the use of the substance bentazone. this substance is commonly used in agriculture and is found in groundwater and surface water throughout europe. in case of doubt about the effects of substances on public health and the environment, the commission cannot propose the approval of substances without a proper investigation.
in writing the active substance bentazone acts as a selective herbicide against broadleaf weeds and is commonly used in agriculture. however, because of its essential properties, bentazone has a high potential to penetrate groundwater, as confirmed by data from the united kingdom environment agency showing that bentazone is the most commonly detected approved pesticide in groundwater in the united kingdom and is also present in surface water; the situation is similar across europe. the precautionary principle to be applied in accordance with regulation (ec) no 1107/2009 requires that the commission does not approve active substances in cases where there is a risk to public health or the environment. there is insufficient information on the safety of the substance bentazone, and an assessment based on representative uses of bentazone is not sufficient to conclude that a plant protection product containing the active substance bentazone will not have adverse effects on human or animal health, on groundwater or on the environment. the commission is therefore going beyond the scope of the implementing powers laid down in the regulation. i therefore support the motion for a resolution in which parliament asks the commission to withdraw its draft implementing regulation and to submit a new proposal to the committee.
in writing ‒ i supported the objection to the re-introduction of the substance bentazone. i do not agree with the procedure adopted by the commission in the authorisation procedure. the authorisation of the active substance benzazone expires on 30 june 2017. however, the commission's proposal envisages extending the authorisation for a further 15 years without taking into account current scientific and technical knowledge. the active substance bentazone is known to be a selective herbicide against broadleaf weeds and is commonly used in agriculture. one of the characteristics of this substance is also its very high potential to penetrate groundwater. bentazone has been detected in groundwater in several countries, however, more detailed information of this nature is missing from the commission proposal. moreover, the consumer risk assessment has not yet been completed. this is because the residue definition for risk assessment in plants and enforcement in livestock was considered provisional due to lack of data. the commission is thus seeking to approve the placing on the market of bentazone before it has a decision confirming its safety. while such a procedure may be used in certain cases, the european ombudsman has already called on the commission to stop applying it to active substances. i therefore believe that the commission will accept this objection and withdraw its proposal.
in writing ‒ an initial risk assessment by the competent authority of the rapporteur member state the netherlands and efsa concluded that the active substance benzazone is safe when used accordingly. herbicides are important for eu agriculture, eu food safety and the toolkit of european farmers and gardeners.

mr. president, when i recently visited jordan, i saw the great impact that the refugee crisis has on the jordanian people. they have received more than 1.4 million syrian refugees and a large group of iraqis and others. i therefore welcome the financial help from the eu to jordan to relieve some of their burden. however, in addition to the macro-financial assistance to help jordan, we should also not forget to help the refugees themselves, including those who are refugees but not registered as such. as i have seen for myself, the eu is helping many refugees, but the problem is that the larger groups of the refugees are either not registered or are not allowed to register. these groups are helped by the jordanian people, churches and ngos. i therefore call on the commission not only to assist jordan at the macro level, but also at the micro level by giving financial assistance to ngos and civil society.
the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a decision on the application of the 'blue card' procedure. - i'm not going to do it. i have a question for you: these carousel transactions, which are created by these frauds, are they not created by the fact that someone in the supply chain can credit the vat and then exports the goods, yes? have you considered that the whole vat system will be replaced by a sales tax, where only the last one, the seller, the non-registered taxpayer, is charged this sales tax, but the registered buyers and suppliers are not charged this tax among themselves? because that would remove the whole basis for the carousel scams.
since 1993, the current vat system has been in force, which is designed as a transitional regime. it was enough time to find out that this system allows for carousel and other frauds in the tens of billions of euros. you can do a lot of things, but the bottom line is that this system allows for carousel fraud. i therefore call on the commission, as well as the council, to change the vat system to a turnover tax system. this means that the individual items in the supply-to-consumer chain will not charge this tax to each other and thus claim it at the same time, which allows for fraud, but only the last item already sold to the final consumer who is not a registered payer of this tax would invoice the tax. this is what's really going to solve these huge problems that we've had here with vat for 20 years.

in writing the current value added tax system in the union was introduced in 1993 as a temporary and transitional system. vat represents a significant and growing revenue stream for member states' budgets and for the eu's own resources. the patterns of tax fraud are changing and often exploit the lack of legislation in this area. i therefore support the proposal that the commission should present by 2017 a definitive value added tax system that is simple, fair, reliable, efficient and at the same time flexible, so as to be able to respond to, eliminate, and effectively investigate and sanction fraud. the practical experience gained so far with the various forms of tax fraud must be the basis for the development of more functional legislation in this area.
in writing. ‒ for any system to work well, monitoring and evaluation are needed periodically. the taxation of trade between member states was now the order of the day. the current system was adopted by the european union in 1993 and was intended to be temporary. i am convinced that we will be able to develop a much more timely and effective regulation.
in writing ‒ i supported the motion for a resolution because i consider the current vat system, especially where it is applied by large corporations to cross-border transactions, to be insufficiently resilient to fraud, tax avoidance strategies, vat non-collection due to insolvency or interpretation. despite the eu and its member states continuing to take measures to combat vat fraud, we continue to see estimates of vat revenue forgone ranging from less than 5% to more than 40%, depending on the country concerned. it is also astonishing to me that member states lose between eur 40 and eur 60 billion of their annual vat revenue as a result of the activities of organised crime groups (the europol incident), seriously undermining their efforts to consolidate public finances. in this context, i therefore agree that we should make even greater efforts, strengthen cooperation between member states and develop comprehensive and integrated anti-fraud strategies, in particular in the face of the current eu budgetary constraints and the growth of e-commerce via the internet, which has weakened territorial controls on vat collection.
in writing ‒ the eu has had a so-called transitional regime in the area of value added tax since 1993. this was to be replaced by a definitive taxation system based on the principle that the supply of goods and services must be taxed in the country of origin. it should be noted that vat is a significant source of finance in the eu and accounts for 7% of the union's gdp. however, the system has often been abused for fraud, as evidenced by the statistics that show that €170 billion is lost annually to tax fraud. cross-border vat fraud is also significant, amounting to eur 50 billion per year. however, the adoption of the new system requires the political will to implement the reforms needed to combat fraud, reduce the administrative burden and reduce regulatory costs. the new vat system could introduce a general taxation obligation on all transactions between economic operators throughout europe, thus significantly strengthening the rules of competition. that's why i supported the report.
in writing wildlife trafficking has become part of international organised crime, which threatens global ecosystems in addition to financial and economic damage and disregard for the rule of law. the union is not only a transit but also a destination for this trade. the profits from this illegal activity also go to fund other criminal activities, including the promotion of terrorism, conflict and power interests. we therefore ask the commission and the member states to adopt the necessary best practices to prevent such activity. we also call on the governments of the supplying countries to stop such trafficking in their countries through thorough investigation, appropriate punishment, eradication of corruption and the establishment of the rule of law.
in writing the wildlife trade is a criminal industry dominated by organised crime groups. the main attraction is the low risk of detection and the high financial reward. the european union is an important player in the fight against wildlife crime, but it is also one of the main markets for illegal endangered species products, as well as a place of transit and often origin for illegal trade in these species. the eu and its member states have a shared responsibility to prevent the rapid loss of some of the world's rarest species. the eu action plan against illicit wildlife trade is part of the eu's response to the un 2030 agenda for sustainable development, in particular sustainable development goal 15, which calls for not only ensuring an end to poaching and illegal trade in protected species, but also addressing the demand for and supply of illegal wildlife products. the first priority of the eu action plan is to prevent wildlife trafficking and to address its causes. the second is to ensure the effective implementation and enforcement of existing rules to combat organised wildlife crime. the third priority is to strengthen the global partnership between countries of origin, consumption and transit in the fight against wildlife trafficking.
in writing. ‒ i fully support the report, as illegal trade in wildlife has a significant negative impact on biodiversity, existing ecosystems, the natural heritage of the countries of origin, natural resources and the protection of species. i believe that trade and development policies should aim to increase respect for human rights, animal welfare and the environment, amongst other things.
in writing ‒ i voted for this resolution. trade in wildlife must be controlled. today, it is dominated by various organized crime groups that take advantage of the low risk of detection and the high profits. i welcome the eu action plan in this area, which has as one of its priorities the prevention of wildlife trafficking, while also considering it necessary to address its causes (e.g. high market demand for illegal products).
in writing ‒ the illegal wildlife trade is one of the most lucrative forms of illicit trade in the world, as an international crime. this is evidenced by the fact that the value of this trade is estimated at eur 20 billion per year and has been increasing in recent years. i voted in favour of the resolution because i believe that we need to take action against illegal wildlife trafficking to ensure the effective implementation and enforcement of existing rules and to strengthen global cooperation between countries of origin and countries of transit and destination. i also supported the action plan because i consider wildlife trafficking to be a very serious threat to global security, political stability and economic development. i hope that, like the eu, individual member states will put in place national wildlife trafficking action plans detailing enforcement policies and sanctions against violators. in this context, i also expect better cooperation between agencies and between stakeholders at both european and national level to prevent wildlife crime.
in writing ‒ i supported the report by mrs bearder on the action plan against illegal wildlife trafficking. the eu action plan, to be fully implemented by 2020, aims in particular to combat these crimes as well as to strengthen the european union's role as a leader in the global fight against illegal activities against wildlife. i agree with the objectives and approach of this action plan. wildlife crime is a matter of transnational concern and its negative impacts on biodiversity, as well as the possible financing of further crime through the proceeds of illegal wildlife trade, should be clearly recognised. this is why states should consider this issue as a matter of political urgency and take a coordinated and effective approach to combating wildlife threatening activities.

in writing. ‒ i have agreed to the proposal to amend an article of the union customs code, as it is a measure which practice has called for. practical problems have been encountered in applying the code to goods temporarily leaving the territory of the union by sea or air. the procedure was simplified, since all the political groups considered the commission proposal to be non-conflictual and therefore no amendments were tabled. the main purpose of the proposal was to simplify the conditions for customs authorities. in order to enable customs authorities to correctly collect import duties, apply non-fiscal measures or identify risks associated with incoming goods, it was necessary to introduce several amendments to the customs code. the provisions incorporated in article 136 of this code concern the lodging of an entry summary declaration, the notification of the arrival of a seagoing vessel, the carriage and presentation of goods after unloading or the obligation to wait for the authorisation before unloading or transhipping the goods. since the proposal is intended only to close this loophole concerning goods which have temporarily left the customs territory of the union, i consider it to be non-problematic. for the overall application of the customs code, these adjustments will provide greater legal certainty for the customs authorities.

in writing. ‒ the since 2002, the european union has operated a solidarity fund whose main objective is to respond to natural disasters in europe and provide financial assistance to the affected states so that they can cope with the consequences of such events more flexibly and quickly. after 12 years of operation, the original regulation was amended in 2014 to better and more accurately reflect the real situation and to speed up the response between the submission of the aid application and the actual granting of funds. however, the european union still has room for improvement in the solidarity fund, for example in prevention and effective post-disaster management. however, prevention must be an integral part of the post-disaster phase. it is important that the restoration of destroyed buildings or repairs to infrastructure facilities provide an opportunity to bring them into line with standards.
in writing. ‒ the the solidarity fund, set up in 2002, is used by the union to help member states and candidate countries cope with the elements. the aid is granted vis-à-vis major, the objective of which is to mitigate the consequences of disasters. the condition is that the total direct damage caused by the natural disaster exceeds eur 3 billion (2011 prices), or 0,6% of the gross national income (gni) of the country concerned. the report points to the need to improve aid management, increase flexibility, increase awareness and at the same time increase transparency in aid delivery.
in writing. - i voted for this resolution. the solidarity fund (established in 2002 after the tragic floods in the eu) is used to express the eu's solidarity with countries affected by major natural disasters. the beneficiary countries may be eu countries or candidate countries for accession. prevention is also an important part of the post-disaster recovery period, in order to avoid damage in future disasters. here cooperation with the cohesion fund is important, where the risk prevention aspect should also be taken into account in infrastructure projects.
in writing. ‒ since its establishment in 2002, the eu solidarity fund has been very useful, mobilising a total of eur 3.8 billion in relation to more than 70 disasters affecting 24 beneficiary and acceding countries and has been used to respond to a variety of natural phenomena, including earthquakes, floods, forest fires, storms and, more recently, drought. it remains one of the strongest symbols of solidarity in times of need. the european solidarity corps is a european union body, which is responsible for providing financial support to the european solidarity corps in the event of a disaster. the new regulation introduces the possibility of granting advance payments of up to 10% of the likely amount of aid, with a maximum of eur 30 million. the solidarity fund should, whenever possible, operate in synergy with other sources of financial assistance, in particular the european structural and investment funds. many natural disasters are caused by climate change, so investments in climate change prevention and mitigation are also needed.

in writing. ‒ i supported the draft decision on the mobilisation of the contingency reserve for 2017. the 2014 mff regulation allows the mobilisation of the reserve up to 0,03 % of the union's gross national income as a last resort to deal with unforeseeable circumstances and should be used only when other funding options have been exhausted. this is precisely the situation that has arisen in the context of the migration, refugee and security crises. since the necessary measures cannot be financed by transferring funds from other budget lines, it is necessary to resort to exceptional instruments, such as the contingency reserve. recognising the scale and gravity of the migration and refugee crisis, i consider it appropriate to mobilise this reserve in order to alleviate it.
